Are we starting to see a shift in the tech contract market? 👀

I saw an interesting stat this week: UK demand for IT contractors reportedly reached its highest level since January 2023 in September, with AI helping drive the increase. 

What I find interesting is that this comes at a time when there is still so much conversation around AI replacing jobs.

From what I’m seeing across Technology, Projects & Change Businesses ARE investing in AI and implementing it properly requires people who can lead programmes, manage change, understand risk and governance.

AI might change the shape of organisations considerably over the next few years, but right now, businesses still need people to implement it, govern it and make sure it actually delivers value.

And that raises an interesting question: for businesses already investing heavily in AI, has headcount actually fallen significantly yet? Or are we simply seeing higher productivity and profitability from the people already there?

Build your ICP in 4 parts.
⠀
After overseeing 300+ GTM motions, we’ve seen that defining what your perfect client looks like is foundational, as it determines all the layers of your GTM:
⠀
- who you make content for
- who you write your emails to
- who your sales reps spend time on
⠀
This is how we do it, in 4 steps:
⠀
1️⃣ Company fit
⠀
 The companies that get the most out of what you sell.
⠀
- What they sell, and to whom
- Headcount and funding stage
- Tools they already pay for
- What your churned accounts have in common
⠀
To map this, you can start with ColdIQ’s research APIs (e.g. Limadata) and data APIs with strong firmographic coverage, like Prospeo.
⠀
> Then, cross-reference it with your CRM data. If you’re already using AI agents like Claude Code, folk is a great option to surface all the information you need in a few prompts.
⠀
2️⃣ User persona
⠀
The person who uses your product every day.
⠀
- Job title and team size
- The number they are judged on
- The words they use to complain
⠀
For example, an SDR Manager running a team of 4 cares about meetings booked per rep, pipeline generated, and how fast new hires ramp.
⠀
Ask yourself, “How do I make him care based on what he does daily?”
⠀
3️⃣ Buyer persona
⠀
The people who sign. Rarely the same person as the user.
⠀
- Who brings you in
- Who signs the contract
- Who can kill the deal
⠀
You can use ColdIQ, where Apollo.io or Prospeo map the buying committee, and your CRM can track every person on the deal.
⠀
In our case, the assumption is that the SDR Manager brings you in, the VP of Sales signs, and Finance checks the budget.
⠀
4️⃣ Signals
⠀
When to reach out.
⠀
- Visits to your pricing page
- Champions who changed jobs
- Hiring, funding, new tools
- The signal that came before your last wins
⠀
You can use PredictLeads to track hiring, funding, and new tools.
⠀
On its own, it indicates good timing. Consider it “Tier 1” when the company, the user, and the buyer also match what you defined above.

Dear Indian IT Industry, Are You Hiring a Fresher or Looking for an Entire IT Department on EMI? 💀
₹3 LPA. That's the salary.
Now, let's see what comes with the package.
The candidate must apparently know #Python, #Java, #C++, #AWS, #Azure, #GCP, #Docker, #Kubernetes, #Jenkins, #Django, #Flask, #SQL, #MongoDB, #Redis, #cybersecurity, VAPT, ML, DL, #GenAI, LLMs, Agentic AI, Microservices, System Design and Advanced DSA.
Are you hiring a software engineer or assembling the Avengers of IT?
And apparently, the online assessment throws a Codeforces 2500+ rated DSA problem at candidates. Because building applications, managing databases, deploying infrastructure and integrating AI isn't enough. Why not add the International Olympiad in Competitive Programming? 😭
BUT WAIT. THE ACTUAL PREMIUM FEATURE:
A THREE-YEAR SERVICE BOND. Want to leave early? Pay ₹3 LAKH.
Quick reality check:
Salary: ₹3 LPA.
Skills: Almost the entire tech ecosystem.
Assessment: Elite-level competitive programming.
Bond: 3 years.
Exit fee: ₹3 lakh.
Sir, are you hiring an employee or acquiring a technology startup?
You want one fresher to build frontend and backend applications, train ML models, integrate LLMs, manage cloud infrastructure, configure CI/CD, handle cybersecurity and design distributed systems.
Anything else? Should they manage HR and make office coffee?
All under one designation. All under one salary. What a steal!
And let's talk about students.
Before graduation, they're already expected to maintain CGPA, master DSA, build projects, complete internships, collect certifications, learn Cloud, AI and DevOps, and gain industry experience.
EXPERIENCE? BEFORE YOUR FIRST JOB? INTERESTING.
Companies want industry-ready candidates, but the entire responsibility of becoming industry-ready falls on students. They spend their own money and time upskilling, yet companies expect them to know everything on Day 1.
So who's supposed to train the fresher? The fresher themselves?
Companies want experience without providing it, expertise without adequate compensation and commitment without necessarily offering the freedom to leave.
At what point does this stop being hiring and start becoming exploitation?
I'm not against hard work, upskilling or challenging interviews. But there's a difference between expecting competence and expecting someone to master an entire technology ecosystem for ₹3 LPA.
A first job should be an opportunity to learn, contribute and grow, NOT a contract to surrender three years of your career for an underpaid opportunity.
A FRESHER IS NOT A DISCOUNTED VERSION OF AN ENTIRE ENGINEERING TEAM.
Dear recruiters, if you're looking for a one-person army, at least budget for the army.
Every thing comes to a single scale of...
NORMALISATION OF EXPLOITING FRESH GRADUATES UNDER THE LABEL OF PROVIDING AN OPPORTUNITY.

Over half the VP placements we make across Europe never have an open job posting on LinkedIn.

There is no application link, no intake form, and no celebratory company announcement that the seat is vacant.

Most senior professionals spend their week refreshing the same public job boards, operating under the assumption that executive hiring runs on volume. Behind the scenes, the most strategic decisions inside a scaleup happen far away from the feed for three operational reasons:

1. Confidential replacement searches.
The company needs to replace an executive who is currently in the seat running day-to-day operations. Going public with the role would destabilize internal teams, spook enterprise clients during contract renewals, and alert competitors.

2. Protecting market narrative.
A scaleup in the middle of a Series B raise or expanding into a new European market cannot afford to signal vulnerability. Broadcasting that you lost your Head of Sales or CTO in the middle of that cycle creates unnecessary friction with investors.

3. The collapse of traditional inbound screening under AI automation.
The moment a senior leadership title goes live on LinkedIn, it attracts 400 generic, bot-generated applications within 48 hours. No serious founder or hiring committee has the bandwidth to sift through automated noise for a €120k+ strategic hire.

The practical takeaway is direct: public job boards show only a fraction of the executive opportunities actually moving in the market.

The most critical conversations happen privately, through structured market mapping and direct outreach to operators who have already proven their ability to deliver at that specific stage of growth.

If your career transition strategy relies entirely on responding to public postings, you are competing in the wrong room.

Build visibility with the people who track your market quietly. At the executive level, the best conversations start months before a job exists on paper.

And then London said no. For nearly six months I couldn’t find a job, and I won’t pretend that was easy. So I taught myself Power BI and Tableau and kept building. John Lewis Partnership gave me a six month contract and a crash course in bulk hiring, until my visa expired and I had to come back to India. 

Coming home was a difficult time. I missed the UK, I wasn’t sure I’d cope, but I kept going. At B4uLeap I got my first taste of tech hiring while we built a GCC, until it was acquired and my role became redundant. 

Then came Abstract Group, where I stopped just recruiting and started building. A talent map across 13 Indian cities. A requisition workflow I built from scratch. KSA market research. Then life threw another curveball, an unfortunate mass layoff closed that chapter at Abstract Group. I just finished Strategic Human Resource Management in the MBA program at Guanghua School of Management, Peking University. 

I went in half expecting HR to be the department that handles contracts and vacation days. I was wrong. The course spent most of its time on a harder question: how a company's people decisions should follow from its strategy, and why so many companies do it the other way around. What stayed with me most is how fast AI is moving into this field. Screening CVs, writing job descriptions, planning onboarding, predicting who might quit next. Work that used to take an HR team weeks now takes a model an afternoon. 
It's also a little scary. A screening model learns from a company's past hiring decisions. If those decisions favored one university, one gender or one type of CV, the model treats that as the definition of a good candidate.
What worries me is the scale. One biased recruiter affects the people they interview. A biased model makes the same mistake thousands of times a day, and the candidates it filters out never learn why.

We were winning work faster than we could deliver it, so I doubled the team in a month, and it felt like the most logical decision I’d ever made. (Just to be clear, this was before the AI Hype)

Within weeks I was drowning, trying to deliver the work and train an army of new hires at the same time. I’d paid for more hands and bought myself a second full-time job, because we’d never built a system for how the work got done.

That’s younger me in the photo and I still love her, she had no grey hairs and looked on point with no sleep and a solid hangover! For many years in business, the flex was how many hours you could work and how big your team was, because that’s what made you a “big” company. These days it’s how efficient you can be, how much tech you can utilise and whether you can get it done from anywhere. (Of course, revenue and profit counts as well)

The old flex dies hard though and we still see the same reflex with clients all the time. A big contract lands, the team is stretched and a job spec starts doing the rounds. More often than not the people they hire are perfectly good, which makes the real problem harder to see.

Be honest with yourself for a second: how much of the way your business runs exists anywhere other than in people’s heads?

Throwing bodies at an un-systematised problem doesn’t fix it, it just gives the chaos more hands. That isn’t a people problem, it’s a design problem.

The method I follow as a founder now is automate, delegate or drop. Before I reach for a new hire, I decide what can be automated, what can be handed to someone who owns it and what shouldn’t be getting done at all. I’m not against hiring, I just follow an order that works exceptionally well for me and my clients.

Headcount doesn’t fix a systems problem, it just makes it more expensive.

What’s the one thing on your plate right now that should already be automated, delegated or dropped? If you need some help deciding, let’s chat.

4 in 10 GitHub PRs now start with an AI agent. 

GitHub's Octoverse report, out last week, says more than 40% of pull requests in September started with an agent. In March it was 17%.

For those of us working remotely from Nigeria, that changes the job. Writing code is getting cheaper. Judging code is not.

I use coding agents every day. The skill that saves me isn't prompting. It's reviewing. And I learnt it teaching beginners at TechyJaunt, reading code that was confident and still wrong.

My review questions are the same for a junior's PR or an agent's:

1. What happens if this runs twice? (webhooks, retries, double charges)
2. What did it change that I didn't ask for? (tests, config, package.json)
3. What happens if the network fails halfway?

If you're job hunting, don't only show what you built. Show a PR where you caught what the agent missed. That tells a hiring manager more than another to-do app.

I'm open to remote senior backend roles and contract work on payments and bookings. My DMs are open.

Thinking about hiring a reverse recruiter for your job search?

Before you pay, understand what the service can actually cost.

In 2026, full-service reverse recruiting can range from roughly:

→ $1,500–$4,000 per month  
→ $1,000–$15,000+ for flat-fee packages  
→ Several thousand dollars for executive programs  
→ Plus, in some cases, 8%–10% of your first-year salary as a success fee  

That last part can become expensive very quickly.

For example:

A 10% success fee on a $100,000 offer = $10,000

A 10% success fee on a $150,000 offer = $15,000

And that may be on top of monthly fees.

So what are you actually paying for?

A reverse recruiter may help with:

• Finding target roles  
• Resume and LinkedIn optimization  
• Submitting applications  
• Hiring-manager outreach  
• Interview preparation  
• Salary negotiation  

But not every provider includes everything.

Before signing a contract, ask:

→ Is there a monthly retainer?  
→ Is there a success fee?  
→ What salary amount is that percentage calculated on?  
→ Is there a minimum commitment?  
→ Are resume and LinkedIn services refundable?  
→ Are there application limits?  
→ What does the guarantee actually mean?  
→ Does “guarantee” mean a refund or simply more service time?  

A reverse recruiter can make sense if:

• You’re targeting senior or executive roles  
• Your search requires networking and direct outreach  
• You have very little time to manage the process  
• You need strategic career support  

But if your biggest problem is simply:

Finding relevant jobs → Tailoring resumes → Submitting applications → Tracking everything

You may not need to spend thousands of dollars.

That’s where application-focused services like FlashFire can be a more affordable alternative.

FlashFire helps with:

→ Finding targeted job opportunities  
→ AI-assisted resume optimization  
→ Job-specific resume tailoring  
→ A team manually submitting applications on your behalf  
→ Tracking applications in one place  
→ Additional career support depending on the plan  

The key is simple:

Don’t pay for a $10,000+ service if you only need help with application execution.

Reverse Recruiter Cost in 2026: Fees, Success Fees and Cheaper Alternatives
